title: The First Call to Prayer
subtitle: The Deliberations of Madinah, the Vision of Abdullah ibn Zayd, and the Voice of Bilal
summary: The dilemma of summoning the growing community to prayer, the consultation rejecting bells, horns, and fires, the true dream granted to Abdullah ibn Zayd and Umar ibn al-Khattab, the appointment of Bilal ibn Rabah, and the resonant anthem of monotheism echoing across Madinah.

sections.text: The Need for a Universal Summons

With the construction of Al-Masjid al-Nabawi complete and the Muslim population multiplying across the scattered groves and settlements of Madinah, a pressing communal challenge presented itself: how to gather the believers for the five daily congregational prayers accurately on time. In the earliest days following the Hijrah, Muslims simply estimated the position of the sun and gathered in anticipation; often, people arrived either too early or missed the opening takbir altogether. A caller would occasionally walk through the alleys shouting 'As-Salatu Jami'ah' (Prayer is assembling), but this method proved inadequate as the city expanded.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ assembled his senior companions in a council of consultation (Shura) to address the issue. Various ideas were proposed: someone suggested striking a wooden clapper or ringing a bell (naqus) after the custom of Christian churches; another proposed blowing a trumpet or ram's horn (shofar) like the Jewish tradition; while a third suggested lighting a beacon fire atop a high hill like the Zoroastrians. The Prophet disliked all these proposals, seeking a method that was distinct, spiritually dignified, and uniquely expressive of monotheistic worship rather than borrowed from other faiths.
The quiet night skies of Madinah where the divine call was revealed in a dream of truth.
The Vision of Abdullah ibn Zayd

That very night, an honorable Ansari companion named Abdullah ibn Zayd ibn Abd Rabbihi retired to his home, his mind deeply occupied with the matter. As he lay in a state between sleep and waking, he witnessed a profound vision. In the dream, a man wearing two green garments approached, carrying a bronze bell in his hand. Abdullah asked: 'O servant of God, will you sell that bell to me?' The man inquired: 'What will you do with it?' Abdullah replied: 'We will strike it to summon the people to prayer.'

The stranger smiled and said: 'Shall I not guide you to that which is far better?' Abdullah eagerly replied: 'Indeed, yes!' The man then stood, faced the Qiblah, and proclaimed in a clear, resonant voice the call, in the wording of Sunan Abi Dawud 499:

اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ، اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ، اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ، اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ
أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ، أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ
أَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ، أَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّدًا رَسُولُ اللَّهِ
حَيَّ عَلَى الصَّلَاةِ، حَيَّ عَلَى الصَّلَاةِ
حَيَّ عَلَى الْفَلَاحِ، حَيَّ عَلَى الْفَلَاحِ
اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ، اللَّهُ أَكْبَرُ
لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ
'God is the greatest, God is the greatest, God is the greatest, God is the greatest. I bear witness that there is no god but God, I bear witness that there is no god but God. I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God, I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God. Come to prayer, come to prayer. Come to success, come to success. God is the greatest, God is the greatest. There is no god but God.' This is the adhan in the transmission of Ibn Ishaq in Abu Dawud 499. Abu Dawud notes that Ma'mar and Yunus, from al-Zuhri, open with 'God is the greatest' twice rather than four times. The testimonies and the two invitations are still repeated. The report is outside Bukhari and Muslim; later graders have called it hasan. The chapter does not enter the dispute over which opening is used in the prayer.
Confirmation and the Selection of Bilal

At daybreak, Abdullah ibn Zayd rushed to the Prophet's Mosque and related his vision in exact detail. The Prophet listened with radiant joy and confirmed: 'Indeed, it is a true vision (Ru'ya haqq), if God wills! Stand alongside Bilal and recite the words to him, so that he may call them out, for indeed he has a louder and more resonant voice than you (fa innahu anda sawtan minka).'

The Prophet's selection of Bilal ibn Rabah carried immense spiritual and historical symbolism. Bilal, the former Ethiopian slave who had been brutally tortured beneath the scorching rocks of Makkah while gasping 'Ahad, Ahad' (One, One), was now elevated to become the first Mu'adhin in Islamic history—the official voice of the faith, calling free men and noble chiefs to bow before the Creator.
The elevated rooftops of early Madinah where the resonant call of Bilal first echoed.
Umar's Corroboration and the Eternal Anthem

Bilal climbed atop the highest roof of a house adjoining the mosque belonging to a woman of Banu Najjar. As the first light of dawn broke over the volcanic hills of Madinah, Bilal raised his powerful, melodious voice, chanting the words taught by Abdullah. The magnificent call rolled across the palm groves, vibrating through every home in the oasis.

Hearing the unfamiliar words echoing through the morning air, Umar ibn al-Khattab sprang from his bed, seized his cloak, and ran through the streets trailing his mantle behind him. Bursting into the mosque before the Prophet, Umar exclaimed: 'By He who sent you with the truth, O Messenger of God! I witnessed the exact same vision in my sleep!' The Prophet smiled with deep gratitude and praised God: 'To God belongs all praise!'

The introduction of the Adhan transformed Islamic worship. It replaced lifeless inanimate instruments with the living human voice, transforming the daily call into an open proclamation of creed, a spiritual reminder, and an invitation to ultimate success. From that blessed morning in Madinah, the words of the Adhan have continued to ring unbroken across every continent and timezone on earth, five times every day.
